description: What machines can compute, what they cannot, and what they cannot compute quickly: automata, grammars, Turing machines, decidability and complexity, with every machine built and run in the simulator. Taught to the depth of the standard automata and complexity course.
modelledOn: Sipser, Introduction to the Theory of Computation
Hopcroft, Motwani and Ullman, Introduction to Automata Theory, Languages, and Computation
Lewis and Papadimitriou, Elements of the Theory of Computation
outcomes: Define languages formally and construct DFAs, NFAs and regular expressions for them and convert between the three.
Prove languages non-regular with the pumping lemma and minimise automata.
Write context-free grammars and pushdown automata and reason about ambiguity and normal forms.
Design Turing machines and explain the Church-Turing thesis and the variants of the model.
Prove problems undecidable by reduction from the halting problem.
Define P, NP, NP-completeness and reductions and classify problems accordingly.

units.title: Alphabets, strings and languages
topics: Alphabets, strings, concatenation, powers, Kleene star; languages as sets of strings
Operations on languages: union, concatenation, star, complement
Proof techniques review: induction, contradiction, diagonalisation, pigeonhole
The Chomsky hierarchy as the map of the course

units.title: Finite automata
topics: Deterministic finite automata: formal definition, transition function, acceptance; designing DFAs
Nondeterministic finite automata and epsilon-transitions; the subset construction
Closure properties of regular languages; product construction
DFA minimisation and the Myhill-Nerode theorem
Applications: lexical analysers, protocol and vending-machine controllers, pattern matching

units.title: Regular expressions and the limits of regularity
topics: Regular expressions: syntax, semantics, algebraic laws
Equivalence of regular expressions and finite automata: Thompson's construction and state elimination
The pumping lemma for regular languages and non-regularity proofs
Decision problems for regular languages: emptiness, membership, equivalence
Regular expressions in practice: grep, validation of phone numbers and Ghana Card IDs

units.title: Context-free grammars
topics: Grammars, derivations, parse trees, leftmost and rightmost derivations; ambiguity
Designing grammars for balanced brackets, arithmetic expressions, palindromes
Chomsky normal form and Greibach normal form; eliminating useless symbols, epsilon and unit productions
The CYK membership algorithm
Pumping lemma for context-free languages; closure and non-closure properties

units.title: Pushdown automata
topics: Pushdown automata: definition, acceptance by final state and by empty stack
Equivalence of PDAs and context-free grammars
Deterministic PDAs and deterministic context-free languages; parsing preview
Decision problems for CFLs

units.title: Turing machines
topics: The Turing machine: definition, configurations, acceptance, recognisers versus deciders
Designing machines for arithmetic and string problems; programming conventions
Variants: multi-tape, nondeterministic, enumerators and their equivalence
The Church-Turing thesis; other models: lambda calculus, random access machines, counter machines
Universal Turing machines and the idea of a stored program
Context-sensitive languages and linear bounded automata in brief

units.title: Decidability and the halting problem
topics: Decidable problems for automata and grammars
Countability, diagonalisation and the existence of unrecognisable languages
The halting problem is undecidable; recognisable but not decidable; co-recognisability
Reductions: proving undecidability of emptiness, equivalence, Rice's theorem
Post correspondence problem; undecidable questions about software (virus detection, program equivalence)

units.title: Complexity classes P and NP
topics: Time complexity of Turing machines; the class P and polynomial-time algorithms
The class NP: verifiers and nondeterministic machines; examples: SAT, clique, Hamiltonian path, subset sum
Polynomial-time reductions; NP-completeness and the Cook-Levin theorem
NP-complete problems and reductions among them; coNP; the P versus NP question
Dealing with hardness: approximation, heuristics, parameterised algorithms; space complexity and PSPACE in brief
Why this matters: cryptography, scheduling, timetabling at a university

schedule.title: Strings, languages and proof techniques
schedule.exercise: Problem set: list the strings of a small language, apply union, concatenation and star to two languages, and prove one claim by induction and one by contradiction.

tasks.title: List all strings of length up to 3 over the alphabet 0,1 and identify those that belong to a given language
Compute the union, concatenation and star (up to length 4) of two small languages, and check closure under each operation
Prove with diagonalisation that the set of infinite binary sequences is uncountable, and show the construction on a given list of sequences

schedule.title: Finite automata
schedule.exercise: Design DFAs for three languages (ending in 01, even number of zeros, divisible by 3) and convert one NFA to a DFA using the subset construction.

tasks.title: Build a DFA that accepts binary strings ending in 01 and run it on eight test strings in the visualiser
Convert an NFA with epsilon moves to an equivalent DFA by the subset construction and verify they agree on twenty strings
Build the product DFA for the intersection of two languages and test it on strings that satisfy one language but not the other

schedule.title: Minimisation and applications of automata
schedule.exercise: Minimise a given 8-state DFA by table-filling, then design a vending-machine or protocol controller as an automaton and test it with five input sequences.

tasks.title: Minimise a 6-state DFA by marking distinguishable pairs and draw the resulting automaton
Design a DFA for a vending machine that accepts coins of 1 and 2 cedis up to 5 and dispenses, and test eight coin sequences
Use the Myhill-Nerode classes to find the minimum number of states for a given language and prove no smaller DFA can exist

schedule.title: Regular expressions and the pumping lemma
schedule.exercise: Convert a regular expression to an NFA by Thompson's construction and back to an expression by state elimination, then prove one language is not regular.

tasks.title: Write regular expressions for three languages, and test each with five accepted and five rejected strings
Convert a regular expression to an NFA by Thompson's construction and then eliminate states to recover an equivalent expression
Prove with the pumping lemma that the language of equal numbers of a and b is not regular, choosing the string and the pumping case

schedule.title: Decision problems and practical regular expressions
schedule.exercise: Write and test a pattern for Ghana phone numbers and Ghana Card ID formats, and give an algorithm to decide emptiness and equivalence of two DFAs.

tasks.title: Decide whether a given DFA accepts any string by checking reachability of an accepting state, and explain the check
Write regular expressions that validate Ghana phone numbers and Ghana Card IDs and test them on 30 valid and invalid strings
Decide equivalence of two DFAs by building their product automaton and searching for a distinguishing string, and test it on three pairs

schedule.title: Context-free grammars
schedule.exercise: Design grammars for balanced brackets, arithmetic expressions and palindromes, show a parse tree for each, and demonstrate ambiguity in one grammar.

tasks.title: Derive a given string by leftmost and rightmost derivations in a grammar and draw its parse tree
Write a grammar for arithmetic expressions with precedence and test it on ten strings including nested brackets
Convert a grammar with epsilon and unit productions to Chomsky normal form step by step, and check the language is unchanged

schedule.title: Membership and non-context-free languages
schedule.exercise: Run the CYK algorithm by hand on a three-rule grammar and a five-letter string, and use the pumping lemma to show that a to the n, b to the n, c to the n is not context-free.

tasks.title: Fill the CYK table for a 5-letter string with a Chomsky normal form grammar and decide membership
Implement the CYK algorithm in code, test it on 20 strings against a known grammar, and report the running time growth
Prove with the pumping lemma for context-free languages that a to the n, b to the n, c to the n is not context-free

schedule.title: Pushdown automata
schedule.exercise: Construct a PDA for the language of palindromes and convert a grammar for balanced brackets into an equivalent PDA, tracing both on test strings.

tasks.title: Run a PDA for a to the n, b to the n on six strings and watch the stack contents during each run
Design a PDA that accepts by empty stack for balanced brackets and test it on ten strings, including invalid ones
Convert a context-free grammar into an equivalent PDA, run both on twenty strings, and explain any strings where they would disagree

schedule.title: Turing machines
schedule.exercise: Design a Turing machine that increments a binary number and one that checks for equal numbers of a and b, giving the full transition table of each.

tasks.title: Run a Turing machine that flips every bit of a binary string, watching the tape, head and state at each step
Design and test a Turing machine that adds one to a binary number, including the carry past the left end
Design a decider for the language of equal numbers of a and b on a single-tape machine, and compare its step count with a two-tape design

schedule.title: Church-Turing thesis and universal machines
schedule.exercise: Explain in a note why a universal Turing machine corresponds to a stored-program computer, and encode one small machine as a string a universal machine could read.

tasks.title: Simulate a counter machine that adds two numbers and show its equivalence to the Turing machine doing the same task
Encode a small Turing machine as a string and trace a universal machine simulating one step of it
Evaluate three terms in the lambda calculus by beta reduction, encode Church numerals for addition, and compare the model with a Turing machine

schedule.title: Decidability and undecidability
schedule.exercise: Prove the halting problem is undecidable, then show by reduction that the emptiness problem for Turing machines is undecidable.

tasks.title: Build the diagonal table for a given list of languages and find a language not on the list
Trace the diagonal argument for the halting problem on a small list of programs and explain the contradiction it produces
Prove by reduction from the halting problem that the equivalence of two Turing machines is undecidable, and explain what Rice's theorem adds

schedule.title: Complexity classes and NP-completeness
schedule.exercise: Show a polynomial-time verifier for subset sum, reduce 3-SAT to clique on a small formula, and explain what a polynomial reduction proves.

tasks.title: Verify a proposed Hamiltonian path in a small graph in polynomial time and explain the verifier's steps
Reduce a small 3-SAT formula to a graph clique problem and check that a satisfying assignment gives a clique of the required size
Prove NP-completeness of independent set by reduction from a known NP-complete problem, and check the construction on a small instance

schedule.title: Coping with hard problems
schedule.exercise: Short essay: choose a timetabling or routing problem and describe an approximation, a heuristic and an exact method, saying what each guarantees.

tasks.title: Solve a small SAT instance by backtracking and count the assignments tried before a solution or a failure
Implement a 2-approximation for vertex cover on random graphs and compare its size with the optimum found by brute force
Build a timetable for a small department with a heuristic and an exact search, and compare quality and time as the problem grows
